claim: Spinal motor neurons serve as one of the best-characterized cell types for addressing how neurons establish individual identity in the developing nervous system and why only specific neuron subtypes are vulnerable to neurodegenerative diseases.
source: In the central nervous system, spinal motor neurons serve as one of the best-characterized cell types for addressing these two questions.
evidence: This is stated directly in the abstract as a characterization of spinal motor neurons' utility in neuroscience research.

claim: The human body contains more than 300 bilateral pairs of muscles and approximately 100 million muscle fibers.
source: The human body contains more than 300 bilateral pairs of muscles and ~100 million muscle fibers.
evidence: This is a direct factual statement about human anatomy provided in the introduction.

claim: Motor neurons can find their original targets even if they have been displaced to another segment of the spinal cord before axonal extension.
source: MNs can find their original targets even if they have been displaced to another segment of the spinal cord before axonal extension, which indicates that most MNs are programmed with an intrinsic identity that encodes information on their targeting preference (Lance-Jones and Landmesser, 1980).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lance-Jones and Landmesser, 1980.

claim: Motor neuron subtypes exhibit differential vulnerability in motor neuron-related degenerative diseases such as amyotrophic lateral sclerosis and spinal muscular atrophy.
source: Moreover, MN subtypes exhibit differential vulnerability in MN-related degenerative diseases that cause progressive muscle weakness and paralysis, such as adult-onset amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS) and childhood spinal muscular atrophy (SMA), further support an intrinsic susceptibility to degeneration amongst MN subtypes.
evidence: This is stated as a known characteristic of motor neuron subtypes in neurodegenerative diseases.

claim: Spinal motor neurons are delineated according to the combinatorial actions of three homeodomain-containing transcription factors: Nkx2.2, Nkx6.1, and Irx3.
source: Spinal MNs are delineated according to the combinatorial actions of three homeodomain-containing transcription factors (TFs) – Nkx2.2, Nkx6.1 and Irx3 – that confine the generation of motor neuron progenitors (pMNs) to the appropriate region of the neural tube (Balaskas et al., 2012; Briscoe et al., 2000)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Balaskas et al., 2012 and Briscoe et al., 2000.

claim: Nkx2.2 and Irx3 initially ensure that motor neuron progenitors are induced in the ventral spinal cord.
source: Nkx2.2 and Irx3 initially ensure that pMNs are induced in the ventral spinal cord.
evidence: This is stated as part of the mechanism of motor neuron progenitor specification.

claim: Nkx6.1 activity promotes the motor neuron progenitor-restricted induction of Olig2.
source: Once pMNs have been defined, Nkx6.1 activity promotes the pMN-restricted induction of downstream factors, such as the basic helix-loop-helix (bHLH) factor Olig2 (Novitch et al., 2001).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Novitch et al., 2001.

claim: Olig2 has a dual role in coordinating the acquisition of pan-neuronal properties and subtype characteristics of differentiating motor neurons.
source: Olig2 has a dual role in coordinating the acquisition of pan-neuronal properties and subtype characteristics of differentiating MNs.
evidence: This is stated as a known function of Olig2 in motor neuron development.

claim: Forced expression of Olig2 in the dorsal region is sufficient to repress Irx3.
source: Forced expression of Olig2 in the dorsal region is sufficient to repress Irx3.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental observation about Olig2 function.

claim: Progenitor domains are determined by a network of transcriptional repressors that repress all inappropriate and alternative cell fates to elicit a single definitive identity.
source: Recent studies have further revealed the gene-regulatory network (GRN) of these progenitor TFs responsible for establishing cell identities in the developing spinal cord, with progenitor domains being determined by a network of transcriptional repressors that repress all inappropriate and alternative cell fates to elicit a single definitive identity (Figure 2A) (Kutejova et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Kutejova et al., 2016.

claim: Olig2 directly represses alternative interneuron domain transcription factors such as Pax6, Irx3, and Nkx2.2.
source: For example, pMN-master regulator Olig2 directly represses alternative interneuron domain TFs such as Pax6, Irx3, and Nkx2.2.
evidence: This is stated as an example of the cross-repressive mechanism in motor neuron progenitors.

claim: In Olig2 mutants, Pax6 and Nkx2.2 are ectopically expanded into motor neuron progenitors.
source: In Olig2 mutants, Pax6 and Nkx2.2 are ectopically expanded into pMNs, supporting the concept of cross-repressive TF-mediated GRN in the pMNs (Balaskas et al., 2012; Zhou and Anderson, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Balaskas et al., 2012 and Zhou and Anderson, 2002.

claim: In anamniotes, maintenance of motor neuron progenitors requires a motor neuron-specific Cyclin Dx (Ccndx).
source: In anamniotes, maintenance of pMNs also requires an MN-specific Cyclin Dx (Ccndx).
evidence: This is stated as a requirement for motor neuron progenitor maintenance in anamniotes.

claim: Inhibition of Ccndx results in specific loss of differentiated motor neurons.
source: Inhibition of Ccndx results in specific loss of differentiated MNs (Chen et al., 2007; Lien et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2007 and Lien et al., 2016.

claim: In mouse embryos, spinal motor neurons acquire generic motor neuron identity after cell cycle exit at about embryonic day 9.5.
source: In mouse embryos, spinal MNs acquire generic MN identity after cell cycle exit (i.e., at about embryonic day 9.5), and express a common set of TFs – Mnx1 (Hb9), Lhx3, Isl1 and Isl2 (Novitch et al., 2001; Thaler et al., 1999; Tsuchida et al., 1994)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Novitch et al., 2001; Thaler et al., 1999; and Tsuchida et al., 1994.

claim: Generic spinal motor neuron identity is established by cooperative binding of the LIM complex comprising Isl1 and Lhx3 to motor neuron-specific enhancers.
source: Generic spinal MN identity is established by cooperative binding of the LIM complex comprising Isl1 and Lhx3 to MN-specific enhancers, thereby inducing the expression of a battery of MN genes that induce functional hallmarks of MNs, while suppressing key interneuron genes.
evidence: This is stated as the mechanism for establishing generic motor neuron identity.

claim: The Isl1-Lhx3 complex amplifies its own expression through a potent autoregulatory feedback loop.
source: Furthermore, the Isl1-Lhx3 complex amplifies its own expression through a potent autoregulatory feedback loop and simultaneously enhances the transcription of Lmo4 to promote MN differentiation and maturation (Erb et al., 2017; Lee et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Erb et al., 2017 and Lee et al., 2012.

claim: Establishment of motor neuron subtype is mediated by mutually exclusive expression of Hox transcription factors programmed according to body segment along the rostrocaudal axis.
source: As embryonic development progresses, MNs diversify to exhibit subtype identities. Establishment of MN subtype is mediated by mutually exclusive expression of Hox TFs, which is programmed according to body segment along the RC axis.
evidence: This is stated as the mechanism for motor neuron subtype specification.

claim: Segmental identity of motor neurons is defined by the mutually exclusive expression of Hox6, Hox9, and Hox10.
source: For example, segmental identity of MNs is defined by the mutually exclusive expression of Hox6, Hox9 and Hox10 (Dasen et al., 2003; Lacombe et al., 2013)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dasen et al., 2003 and Lacombe et al., 2013.

claim: Hoxc9 is required for the generation of thoracic motor neuron subtypes and is essential for organizing the motor neuron topographic map.
source: In particular, a single Hox gene, Hoxc9, required for the generation of thoracic MN subtypes, is essential for organizing the MN topographic map, and acts as a key repressor of the forelimb-level Hox network (Jung et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jung et al., 2010.

claim: Within the brachial segment hosting Hox6 expression, motor neurons are grouped into axial muscle-projecting motor neurons (Lhx3on, MMC) and forelimb-innervating motor neurons (Foxp1on, LMC).
source: For instance, within the brachial segment hosting Hox6 expression, MNs are further grouped into axial muscle-projecting MNs (Lhx3on, MMC) and forelimb-innervating MNs (Foxp1on, LMC)(Dasen et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Dasen et al., 2008.

claim: Expression of Hox5 and Hox8 in Foxp1on LMC controls the rostral and caudal motor pool identity, which directs motor pools to innervate either proximal or distal muscles in the forelimb.
source: Within Hoxc6on MNs, expression of another set of mutually exclusive Hox proteins, such as Hox5 and Hox8 in Foxp1on LMC, controls the rostral and caudal motor pool identity, which directs motor pools to either innervate proximal or distal muscles in the forelimb (Catela et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Catela et al., 2015.

claim: Only Hoxc8 represses Hoxa5 unilaterally at protein level, despite a mutually exclusive Hoxa5-Hoxc8 sharp boundary being manifested within the Hoxc6on motor neurons.
source: Although a mutually exclusive expressed Hoxa5-Hoxc8 sharp boundary is manifested within the Hoxc6on MNs, unlike progenitor-TFs that display mutual inhibitions, only Hoxc8 represses Hoxa5 unilaterally at protein level (Dasen et al., 2005; Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dasen et al., 2005 and Li et al., 2017.

claim: LMC is further classified into divisional identities targeting flexor and extensor limb muscles.
source: LMC is the most extensively studied motor column, and this motor column is further classified into divisional identities targeting flexor and extensor limb muscles (Kania and Jessell, 2003; Sockanathan and Jessell, 1998).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Kania and Jessell, 2003 and Sockanathan and Jessell, 1998.

claim: Motor neurons labeled by retrograde labeling of each muscle group occupy distinct and stereotyped positions in the spinal cord.
source: Further heterogeneity in spinal MNs can be revealed by retrograde labeling of each muscle group, with labeled MNs occupying distinct and stereotyped positions in the spinal cord (Hollyday, 1980a; Hollyday, 1980b; Landmesser, 1978a; Landmesser, 1978b; McHanwell and Biscoe, 1981; Romanes, 1964; Sürmeli et al., 2011; Vanderhorst and Holstege, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations to studies using retrograde labeling.

claim: Loss-of-function studies of Nkx6.1 and Nkx6.2 have resulted in target innervation and arborization defects in adductor and gracilis muscles.
source: For example, Nkx6.1 and Nkx6.2 are expressed in subpopulations of MNs and loss-of-function studies of these proteins have resulted in target innervation and arborization defects in adductor and gracilis muscles (De Marco Garcia and Jessell, 2008; Ghosh and Kolodkin, 1998; Livet et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to De Marco Garcia and Jessell, 2008; Ghosh and Kolodkin, 1998; and Livet et al., 2002.

claim: Expression of the ETS-TF Etv4 (Pea3) in motor neurons innervating cutaneous maximus and latissimus dorsi muscles in the forelimb requires GDNF signal activation from the periphery.
source: In addition, extrinsic cues are also indispensable for precisely defining MN subtype diversification and axon targeting. For example, expression of the ETS-TF Etv4 (Pea3) in MNs innervating cutaneous maximus and latissimus dorsi muscles in the forelimb requires GDNF signal activation from the periphery (Haase et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Haase et al., 2002.

claim: Cpne4/Fign markers and evasion of non-canonical retinoic acid signaling label the motor neuron subtype innervating digit muscles.
source: Recently, Jessell and colleagues revealed that Cpne4/Fign markers and evasion of non-canonical retinoic acid signaling label the MN subtype innervating digit muscles, providing insights into the emergence of a divergent molecular program during evolution (Mendelsohn et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Mendelsohn et al., 2017.

claim: 60 motor pools are thought to exist in either the brachial or lumbar LMC motor neurons innervating mouse limb muscles.
source: Even though 60 motor pools are thought to exist in either the brachial or lumbar LMC-MNs innervating mouse limb muscles, a complete subtype-specific gene profile for each motor pool is still lacking, not to mention for the other less well-profiled motor columns (D'Elia and Dasen, 2018; Fetcho, 1987)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to D'Elia and Dasen, 2018 and Fetcho, 1987.

claim: More than one-third of the genes in the human genome might be regulated by microRNAs.
source: It has been proposed that more than one-third of the genes in the human genome might be regulated by miRNAs (Lewis et al., 2005).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lewis et al., 2005.

claim: miR-17–3p is required to silence transient Olig2 expression in p2 progenitors.
source: By disrupting miRNA biogenesis during simulated DV patterning of differentiating ES cells both in cellulo and in vivo, it was revealed that miR-17–3p, a member of the miR-17 ~92 cluster, is required to silence transient Olig2 expression in p2 progenitors (Chen et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen et al., 2011.

claim: Specific timing of miR-196 expression is required for proper motor neuron differentiation, which is mediated by downregulation of Hoxb8.
source: In the developing spinal cord of chick embryos, specific timing of miR-196 expression is required for proper MN differentiation, which is mediated by downregulation of Hoxb8.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from studies in chick embryos.

claim: Failure to clear Hoxb8 in a spatial and temporal manner abolishes motor neuron generation.
source: Failure to clear Hoxb8 in a spatial and temporal manner abolishes MN generation (Asli and Kessel, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Asli and Kessel, 2010.

claim: In conditional neural Dicer mutants, Hoxa5 protein is precociously expressed at progenitors and the Hox5/8 boundary is expanded caudally.
source: In conditional neural Dicer mutants (Sox1-Cre; Dicerfloxed, Dicer NeuralΔ ) in which all mature miRNA production is abrogated in the CNS, Hoxa5 protein is precociously expressed at progenitors and the Hox5/8 boundary is expanded caudally, both in cellulo and in vivo (Figure 3B) (Li et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Li et al., 2017 and reference to Figure 3B.

claim: miR-27 is a major regulator coordinating the temporal delay and spatial boundary of Hox protein expression.
source: Using in silico simulation, two feed-forward Hox-miRNA loops have been uncovered that account for the precocious and noisy Hoxa5 expression, as well as the ill-defined boundary phenotype of Dicer mutants. In this scenario, miR-27 appears to be a major regulator coordinating the temporal delay and spatial boundary of Hox protein expression.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from in silico simulation studies.

claim: Expression of miR-218 is directly upregulated by the Isl1-Lhx3 complex to drive motor neuron fate.
source: In the developing spinal cord, expression of miR-218 is directly upregulated by the Isl1-Lhx3 complex to drive MN fate (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated as a mechanism of miR-218 regulation in motor neuron development.

claim: Loss of miR-218 function leads to impaired generation of generic motor neurons.
source: Loss of miR-218 function leads to impaired generation of generic MNs, suggesting that this miRNA plays a crucial role in MN differentiation (Amin et al., 2015; Thiebes et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Amin et al., 2015 and Thiebes et al., 2015.

claim: Mutant mice lacking miR-218 die neonatally and exhibit neuromuscular junction defects, motor neuron hyperexcitability, and progressive motor neuron degeneration.
source: Furthermore, mutant mice lacking miR-218 die neonatally and exhibit neuromuscular junction defects, MN hyperexcitability, and progressive MN degeneration, recapitulating traits of motor neuron disease (Amin et al., 2015).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Amin et al., 2015.

claim: miR-218 represses an array of transcripts in the alternative neighboring interneuron genes to maintain postmitotic motor neuron cell fate and robust neuromuscular functions.
source: However, miR-218 does not seem to exert its functions by targeting a few specific genes. Instead, it appears to repress an array of transcripts in the alternative neighboring interneuron genes to maintain postmitotic MN cell fate and robust neuromuscular functions (Amin et al., 2015; Thiebes et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Amin et al., 2015 and Thiebes et al., 2015.

claim: miR-218 is encoded by an intron of the extracellular matrix Slit2 and Slit3 genes.
source: Interestingly, miR-218 is encoded by an intron of the extracellular matrix Slit2 and Slit3 genes and it inhibits expression of neural cell adhesion molecules Robo1 and Robo2 and multiple components of the heparan sulfate biosynthetic pathway responsible for normal vascularization of the retina (Small et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Small et al., 2010.

claim: miR-9 is transiently expressed in Foxp1on LMC regions.
source: For instance, miR-9 is transiently expressed in Foxp1on LMC regions.
evidence: This is stated as an observation about miR-9 expression pattern.

claim: Overexpression or knockdown of miR-9 alters motor neuron subtypes, switches columnar identities, and changes axonal innervations in developing chick spinal cords.
source: Overexpression or knockdown of miR-9 alters MN subtypes, switches columnar identities, and changes axonal innervations in developing chick spinal cords.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding in chick spinal cords.

claim: miR-9 modifies spinal columnar organization by specifically regulating Foxp1 protein levels.
source: miR-9 modifies spinal columnar organization by specifically regulating Foxp1 protein levels, which in turn determine distinct MN subtypes (Otaegi et al., 2011)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Otaegi et al., 2011.

claim: Deletion of Dicer from all motor neurons using Olig2-Cre revealed a preferential loss of many limb- and sympathetic ganglia-innervating spinal motor neurons.
source: Additionally, deletion of the enzyme Dicer from all MNs using Olig2-Cre (Dicer MNΔ ) revealed a preferential loss of many limb- and sympathetic ganglia-innervating spinal MNs (Chen and Wichterle, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Chen and Wichterle, 2012.

claim: Disruption of Dicer in motor neurons led to defects in motor pool identity specification.
source: Furthermore, this disruption also led to defects in motor pool identity specification, yet the miRNA candidates to maintain motor pool identity have yet to be unveiled (Figure 3D).
evidence: This is stated as a finding from Dicer deletion studies.

claim: The miR-17~92 cluster is highly enriched in LMC motor neurons.
source: Subsequent study uncovered that the miR-17 ~92 cluster is highly enriched in LMC-MNs.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from subsequent studies.

claim: Conditional motor neuron miR-17~92 deletion resulted in selective cell death of LMC motor neurons.
source: Furthermore, conditional MN miR-17 ~92 deletion (mi-17 ~92 MNΔ ) resulted in selective cell death of LMC-MNs.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding.

claim: miR-17~92 not only suppresses PTEN expression, but also independently attenuates accumulation of nuclear PTEN.
source: Mechanistically, mir-17 ~92 not only suppresses PTEN expression, but also independently attenuates accumulation of nuclear PTEN, with this latter being a more potent apoptosis stimulator (Tung et al., 2015)
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tung et al., 2015.

claim: Reduced miR-17~92 is accompanied by elevated nuclear PTEN in the spinal motor neurons of presymptomatic SOD1G93A mice.
source: Tellingly, reduced miR-17 ~92 is accompanied by elevated nuclear PTEN in the spinal MNs of presymptomatic SOD1G93A mice, that is the most common mouse strain used as an ALS disease model.
evidence: This is stated as an observation in the ALS mouse model.

claim: Overexpression of miR-17~92 significantly rescues human SOD1+/L144F motor neurons.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of miR-17 ~92 significantly rescues human SOD1+/L144F MNs, and intrathecal delivery of scAAV9 [self-complementary adeno-associated viral serotype 9]-miR-17 ~ 92 improves motor deficits and survival in SOD1G93A mice (Tung et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tung et al., 2019.

claim: Intrathecal delivery of scAAV9-miR-17~92 improves motor deficits and survival in SOD1G93A mice.
source: Furthermore, overexpression of miR-17 ~92 significantly rescues human SOD1+/L144F MNs, and intrathecal delivery of scAAV9 [self-complementary adeno-associated viral serotype 9]-miR-17 ~ 92 improves motor deficits and survival in SOD1G93A mice (Tung et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Tung et al., 2019.

claim: SMA is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disease characterized by devastating muscular atrophy attributable to progressive spinal motor neuron degeneration.
source: SMA is an autosomal recessive neurodegenerative disease characterized by devastating muscular atrophy attributable to progressive spinal MN degeneration.
evidence: This is a standard definition of SMA provided in the text.

claim: SMA has an estimated worldwide incidence of one in 6,000 to 10,000 newborns.
source: Although SMA is a relatively rare disease, with an estimated worldwide incidence of one in 6,000 ~ 10,000 newborns, it is notable that SMA is the second most common autosomal recessive disease after cystic fibrosis and is the most common monogenic defect leading to infant mortality (Lunn and Wang, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lunn and Wang, 2008.

claim: SMA is the second most common autosomal recessive disease after cystic fibrosis.
source: Although SMA is a relatively rare disease, with an estimated worldwide incidence of one in 6,000 ~ 10,000 newborns, it is notable that SMA is the second most common autosomal recessive disease after cystic fibrosis and is the most common monogenic defect leading to infant mortality (Lunn and Wang, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lunn and Wang, 2008.

claim: SMA is the most common monogenic defect leading to infant mortality.
source: Although SMA is a relatively rare disease, with an estimated worldwide incidence of one in 6,000 ~ 10,000 newborns, it is notable that SMA is the second most common autosomal recessive disease after cystic fibrosis and is the most common monogenic defect leading to infant mortality (Lunn and Wang, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Lunn and Wang, 2008.

claim: SMA is caused by reduced levels of the 38 kDa Survival Motor Neuron (SMN) protein due to deletion or mutation of the Survival of Motor Neuron 1 (SMN1) gene.
source: SMA is caused by reduced levels of the 38 kDa Survival Motor Neuron (SMN) protein due to deletion or mutation of the Survival of Motor Neuron 1 (SMN1) gene.
evidence: This is stated as the genetic cause of SMA.

claim: SMN protein is encoded by two genes in humans: SMN1 and highly homologous SMN2, which differ by one nucleotide (C→T) in exon 7.
source: In humans, SMN protein is actually encoded by two genes: SMN1 and highly homologous SMN2, which essentially differs by one nucleotide (C→T) in exon 7.
evidence: This is stated as a fact about human SMN genes.

claim: The C→T nucleotide difference in exon 7 of SMN2 results in preferential exclusion of exon seven from most SMN2 transcripts.
source: This critical difference results in preferential exclusion of exon seven from most SMN2 transcripts, termed SMN△7.
evidence: This is stated as a consequence of the nucleotide difference.

claim: SMN2 generates approximately 10% of full-length SMN mRNAs and their product-functional SMN proteins.
source: As a consequence, SMN2 generates ~10% of full-length (FL) SMN mRNAs and their product-functional SMN proteins (Burghes and Beattie, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Burghes and Beattie, 2009.

claim: The full-length SMN2 transcript copy number may determine phenotypic severity in SMA patients.
source: As these FL-SMN2 transcripts can partially compensate for loss of SMN1, it is reasoned that the FL-SMN2 transcript copy number may determine phenotypic severity in SMA patients.
evidence: This is stated as a reasoning about SMA phenotypic severity.

claim: Additional modifiers might be involved in modulating SMA clinical severity beyond SMN2 copy number.
source: However, recent studies have indicated that additional modifiers might also be involved in modulating SMA clinical severity (Crawford et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Crawford et al., 2012.

claim: SMN is ubiquitously expressed in almost all kinds of somatic cells, with a distribution in both the cytoplasm and nucleus.
source: SMN is ubiquitously expressed in almost all kinds of somatic cells, with a distribution in both the cytoplasm and nucleus (Burghes and Beattie, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Burghes and Beattie, 2009.

claim: The most appreciated canonical role of SMN is to serve as an essential ribonucleoprotein for mRNA splicing.
source: Notably, the most appreciated canonical role of SMN is to serve as an essential ribonucleoprotein (RNP) for mRNA splicing.
evidence: This is stated as the canonical role of SMN.

claim: SMN protein is embedded in a complex with seven Gemins and UNRIP that loads Sm protein onto nascent U-snRNAs upon their export to the cytoplasm.
source: SMN protein is embedded in a complex with seven Gemins and UNR-interacting protein (UNRIP) that loads Sm protein onto nascent uridine-rich noncoding RNAs (U-snRNAs) upon their export to the cytoplasm, thereby creating small nuclear RNPs (snRNPs) that form spliceosomes in the nucleus (Burghes and Beattie, 2009; Dostie et al., 2003).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Burghes and Beattie, 2009 and Dostie et al., 2003.

claim: The SMN complex has a role in assisting arginine methylation of some splicing-related proteins involved in pre-mRNA splicing.
source: In addition to facilitating snRNP assembly, the SMN complex has a role in assisting arginine methylation of some splicing-related proteins that are involved in pre-mRNA splicing (Meister and Fischer, 2002; Pellizzoni et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Meister and Fischer, 2002 and Pellizzoni et al., 2002.

claim: There is a direct correlation between the ability to assemble snRNPs and SMA phenotypes in animal models.
source: Studies on SMA animal models have also revealed a direct correlation between the ability to assemble snRNPs and SMA phenotypes, and delivery of mature snRNPs even without the SMN component is sufficient to rescue SMA phenotypes (Gabanella et al., 2007; Winkler et al., 2005; Workman et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gabanella et al., 2007; Winkler et al., 2005; and Workman et al., 2009.

claim: Delivery of mature snRNPs without the SMN component is sufficient to rescue SMA phenotypes.
source: Studies on SMA animal models have also revealed a direct correlation between the ability to assemble snRNPs and SMA phenotypes, and delivery of mature snRNPs even without the SMN component is sufficient to rescue SMA phenotypes (Gabanella et al., 2007; Winkler et al., 2005; Workman et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Gabanella et al., 2007; Winkler et al., 2005; and Workman et al., 2009.

claim: SMN protein levels might affect splicing of SMN pre-mRNA to include exon seven through an autoregulatory loop.
source: This outcome implies that SMN protein levels might affect splicing of SMN pre-mRNA to include exon seven through an autoregulatory loop, thereby influencing a general process of snRNP biogenesis (Jodelka et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Jodelka et al., 2010.

claim: Assembly of SMN protein is involved in DNA repair and protein/mRNA transportation along motor neuron axons.
source: For example, assembly of SMN protein is also involved in a number of essential cellular pathways, including DNA repair and protein/mRNA transportation along MN axons (Donlin-Asp et al., 2016; Fallini et al., 2012; Murray et al., 2015; Tu et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Donlin-Asp et al., 2016; Fallini et al., 2012; Murray et al., 2015; and Tu et al., 2017.

claim: Deletion of the miRNA biogenesis enzyme Dicer in motor neurons results in motor neuron degeneration that mimics certain hallmarks of SMA and ALS.
source: Deletion of the miRNA biogenesis enzyme Dicer in MNs either using Olig2-Cre or ChAT-Cre results in MN degeneration that mimics certain hallmarks of SMA and ALS (Chen and Wichterle, 2012; Haramati et al., 2010; Tung et al., 2019).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen and Wichterle, 2012; Haramati et al., 2010; and Tung et al., 2019.

claim: Gemin3 and Gemin4 of the SMN complex can assemble with a number of miRNAs to form a miRNA-binding RNP (miRNP).
source: For example, Gemin3 and Gemin4 of the SMN complex can assemble with a number of miRNAs to form a miRNA-binding RNP (miRNP) (Dostie et al., 2003; Mourelatos et al., 2002)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dostie et al., 2003 and Mourelatos et al., 2002.

claim: The miRNP complex can bind to Argonaute 2 (AGO2) that functions as a core protein in the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) mediating miRNA biogenesis and mRNA posttranscriptional regulation.
source: This miRNP complex can further bind to Argonaute 2 (AGO2) that functions as a core protein in the RNA-induced silencing complex (RISC) mediating miRNA biogenesis as well as mRNA posttranscriptional regulation (Cauchi, 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Cauchi, 2010.

claim: SMN interacts with miRNA biogenesis proteins including FMRP, KSRP, and FUS/TLS.
source: Interestingly, in addition to the role of SMN in RNA processing, recent studies have uncovered unexpected interactions of SMN with miRNA biogenesis proteins including fragile X mental retardation protein (FMRP), KH‐type splicing regulatory protein (KSRP) and fused in sarcoma/translocated in liposarcoma (FUS/TLS) (Piazzon et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2015; Tadesse et al., 2008; Yamazaki et al., 2012)
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Piazzon et al., 2008; Sun et al., 2015; Tadesse et al., 2008; and Yamazaki et al., 2012.

claim: Deficiency of SMN may alter motor neuron-specific miRNAs or miRNPs, resulting in motor neuron death.
source: Thus, SMN is engaged in miRNA–RBP complexes and likely regulates miRNA biogenesis and metabolism. Deficiency of SMN may alter MN-specific miRNAs or miRNPs, resulting in MN death (Cauchi, 2010; Nelson et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Cauchi, 2010 and Nelson et al., 2004.

claim: Reduced SMN activity specifically affects miR-2 expression, which causes motor neurons to produce more m2R, a receptor for acetylcholine.
source: By using both mouse and nematode models of SMA, O' Hern et al. showed that reduced SMN activity specifically affects miR-2 expression, which in turn causes MNs to produce more m2R, a receptor for acetylcholine (O'Hern et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to O'Hern et al., 2017.

claim: SMN protein levels in astrocytes affect both directly and indirectly altered expression levels of miR-146a.
source: Interestingly, it was recently shown that SMN protein levels in astrocytes affect both directly and indirectly altered expression levels of miR-146a (Sison et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Sison et al., 2017.

claim: Increased levels of miR-146a in the SMNΔ7 mouse spinal cord are linked to astrocyte-mediated SMA pathology.
source: The proposed mechanism for that astrocyte-mediated SMA pathology was linked to increased levels of miR-146a in the SMNΔ7 mouse spinal cord.
evidence: This is stated as a proposed mechanism for SMA pathology.

claim: Treating iPSC-derived motor neurons with synthesized miR-146a molecules was sufficient to induce significant motor neuron loss.
source: Although the precise targets of miR-146a have not yet been identified, treating iPSC-derived MNs with synthesized miR-146a molecules was sufficient to induce significant MN loss.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding.

claim: Two undergoing SMA treatment trials using antisense oligonucleotides or virus-mediated gene therapy exhibited promising outcomes.
source: Two undergoing SMA treatment trials either use antisense oligonucleotides or virus-mediated gene therapy exhibited promising outcomes (Finkel et al., 2017; Mendell et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Finkel et al., 2017 and Mendell et al., 2017.

claim: Mendell et al. used single intravenous administration of nonreplicating scAAV9 adenovirus vector carrying a human wild type SMN1 sequence for SMA treatment.
source: Mendell et al. used single intravenous administration of nonreplicating scAAV9 adenovirus vector carrying a human wild type SMN1 sequence.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the treatment approach used by Mendell et al.

claim: Finkel et al. applied an antisense approach designed to enhance inclusion of exon seven in SMN2, involving repetitive intrathecal administration of the antisense oligonucleotide drug Nusinersen.
source: In contrast, Finkel et al. applied an antisense approach that was designed to enhance inclusion of exon seven in SMN2, which involved repetitive intrathecal administration of the antisense oligonucleotide drug Nusinersen.
evidence: This is stated as a description of the treatment approach used by Finkel et al.

claim: Quantification of SMN mRNA or protein levels does not necessarily correlate with disease severity and may not reliably reflect disease progression in SMA.
source: Quantification of SMN mRNA or protein levels has served as the most commonly used molecular biomarker of SMA, but it does not necessarily correlate with disease severity and may not reliably reflect disease progression (Sumner et al., 2006; Wadman et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Sumner et al., 2006 and Wadman et al., 2016.

claim: MiRNAs are clinically detectable in many biofluids such as cerebrospinal fluid, serum/plasma, saliva, and urine using noninvasive methods.
source: MiRNAs have gained attention as an easily accessible biomarker due to their characteristic of being clinically detectable in many biofluids - such as cerebrospinal fluid, serum/plasma, saliva, and urine - using noninvasive methods (Viswambharan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Viswambharan et al., 2017.

claim: miR-9, miR-132, miR-206, miR-183, and miR-375 have been proposed as potentially reliable SMA biomarkers.
source: As summarized in Table 2, miR-9, miR-132, miR-206, miR-183 and miR-375 have been proposed as potentially reliable SMA biomarkers (Israeli et al., 2016; Perry and Muntoni, 2016; Viswambharan et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Israeli et al., 2016; Perry and Muntoni, 2016; and Viswambharan et al., 2017.

claim: A recent phase 3 study of an antisense oligonucleotide treatment for severe infantile SMA revealed quite distinct responses among patients.
source: Notably, a recent phase 3 study of an antisense oligonucleotide treatment for severe infantile SMA revealed quite distinct responses among patients (Finkel et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by a citation to Finkel et al., 2017.

claim: The time between recording the first symptoms in type I SMA patients and initial delivery of the antisense oligonucleotide was identified as a factor influencing treatment response.
source: In that study, the only factor identified as influencing treatment response was the time between recording the first symptoms in type I SMA patients and initial delivery of the antisense oligonucleotide.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the phase 3 study.

claim: Using a scAAV9 viral vector to reintroduce mir-23a into the Smn2B/- SMA mouse model increased motor neuron size, reduced neuromuscular junction pathology, and extended survival.
source: However, using a scAAV9 viral vector to reintroduce mir-23a into the Smn2B/- SMA mouse model increased MN size, reduced neuromuscular junction (NMJ) pathology, and extended survival.
evidence: This is stated as an experimental finding.

claim: Kaifer et al. identified a subset of 16 miRNAs whose expression is significantly reduced more than 2-fold in SMA motor neurons compared to control motor neurons.
source: In that study, Kaifer et al. only identified a subset of 16 miRNAs whose expression is significantly reduced more than 2-fold in SMA MNs when compared to control MNs.
evidence: This is stated as a finding from the Kaifer et al. study.

claim: Approximately 5 miRNAs are highly or specifically expressed in motor neurons.
source: Although ~5 miRNAs are highly or specifically expressed in MNs, only two mouse knockout lines (i.e., miR-17 ~92MNΔ and a miR-218 double knockout) have been characterized in detail.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of miRNA expression in motor neurons.

claim: Only two mouse knockout lines (miR-17~92MNΔ and miR-218 double knockout) have been characterized in detail for motor neuron-specific miRNAs.
source: Although ~5 miRNAs are highly or specifically expressed in MNs, only two mouse knockout lines (i.e., miR-17 ~92MNΔ and a miR-218 double knockout) have been characterized in detail.
evidence: This is stated as a summary of characterized mouse knockout lines.

claim: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved the first drug utilizing RNA interference for adult clinical treatment of hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis.
source: Finally, twenty years after the breakthrough discovery illustrating how RNA interference can be used to silence certain genes, the U.S. Food and Drug Administration has approved the first drug utilizing this method for adult clinical treatment of a rare disease (i.e., hereditary transthyretin-mediated amyloidosis).
evidence: This is stated as a fact about FDA approval.

claim: Limb-innervating motor neurons are located in the lateral motor columns at brachial and lumbar levels.
source: Limb-innervating MNs are located in the lateral motor columns (LMC) at brachial and lumbar levels, whereas preganglionic (PGC) and hypaxial (HMC) neurons at thoracic levels innervate the sympathetic ganglia and hypaxial muscles, respectively.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Preganglionic and hypaxial neurons at thoracic levels innervate the sympathetic ganglia and hypaxial muscles, respectively.
source: Limb-innervating MNs are located in the lateral motor columns (LMC) at brachial and lumbar levels, whereas preganglionic (PGC) and hypaxial (HMC) neurons at thoracic levels innervate the sympathetic ganglia and hypaxial muscles, respectively.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: Medial motor neurons are distributed at all rostrocaudal levels and project dorsally to epaxial muscles.
source: Medial motor (MMC) neurons are distributed at all rostrocaudal levels and project dorsally to epaxial muscles.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 1A.

claim: A gradient of Sonic hedgehog protein emanating from the notochord and floor plate, together with BMP/TGFβ signaling from the roof plate, mediates repression of class I homeodomain proteins and induction of class II protein expression at different threshold concentrations.
source: Upon neural tube closure, a gradient of Sonic hedgehog protein (Shh) emanating from the notochord (NC) and floor plate (FP), together with BMP/TGFβ signaling from the roof plate (RP), mediates repression of class I homeodomain proteins (e.g. Irx3 and Pax6) and induction of class II protein expression (e.g. Nkx6.1 and Nkx2.2) at different threshold concentrations.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Retinoic acid is expressed by the paraxial mesoderm to induce expression of class I proteins.
source: Retinoic acid (RA) is expressed by the paraxial mesoderm to induce expression of class I proteins, which are turned off more ventrally by threshold levels of Shh.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Shh signaling defines five progenitors (p0-p3 and pMN) that give rise to V0-V3 interneurons and motor neurons.
source: Shh signaling defines five progenitors (p0-p3 and pMN) that give rise to V0-V3 interneurons and motor neurons.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2A.

claim: Fibroblast growth factor signals maintain a caudal progenitor zone during axis extension.
source: Fibroblast growth factor (FGF) signals maintain a caudal progenitor zone during axis extension, and down-regulation of FGF signaling by RA is required for neuronal patterning and differentiation at more rostral levels.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2C.

claim: Down-regulation of FGF signaling by RA is required for neuronal patterning and differentiation at more rostral levels.
source: Fibroblast growth factor (FGF) signals maintain a caudal progenitor zone during axis extension, and down-regulation of FGF signaling by RA is required for neuronal patterning and differentiation at more rostral levels.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2C.

claim: The RA and FGF gradient elicits expression of Hox genes along the rostrocaudal axis.
source: The RA and FGF gradient elicits expression of Hox genes along the rostrocaudal axis.
evidence: This claim is stated in the text and illustrated in Figure 2C.
